Subject: Trail etiquette: a quick refresher before you head out
CTA: Read more trail resources on our site -> https://www.northbaysupply.com/trail-resources
Body: Hey,

You already know how to read a topo map and layer for weather. This isn't that kind of guide. But trail etiquette is one of those things that's easy to let slide — especially when you're deep in trip-planning mode and your head is full of mileage and gear lists.

So here's a plain-language refresher. Pass it along if it's useful.

---

YIELD ORDER

The standard hierarchy on mixed-use trails: hikers yield to horses, bikes yield to hikers, everyone yields to horses. When in doubt, step to the side, make yourself visible, and let the other party pass. On equestrian trails, move to the downhill side and speak calmly so horses can locate you by sound.

---

UPHILL RIGHT-OF-WAY

Give way to people climbing. They're working harder, they've likely broken their rhythm, and stopping on a steep grade is harder than it sounds. Step aside, let them through, exchange a nod.

---

STAY ON TRAIL

Cutting switchbacks damages vegetation and accelerates erosion. It's faster for you and worse for everyone who comes after. If the trail is muddy, walk through it — not around it. Widening the trail compounds the problem.

---

LEAVE NO TRACE (THE SHORT VERSION)

Pack out everything you packed in. Human waste should be buried 6 to 8 inches deep in a cat hole, at least 200 feet from water, trails, and camp. Wag bags are worth carrying in areas with high use or fragile soil. Don't leave orange peels or apple cores — they take longer to decompose than people assume and they alter local wildlife behavior.

---

NOISE AND SPACE

Keep group sizes manageable. Most wilderness areas cap permit groups at 12; many recommend fewer. Music through a speaker affects everyone within earshot. Earbuds keep the trail quiet for others and keep you aware of what's around you.

---

PASS WITH INTENTION

If you're moving faster than the group ahead, say something before you're right behind them. A simple "on your left" or "passing when you're ready" is enough. Startling someone on a narrow ridge is avoidable.

---

CAMPSITE SELECTION

In areas without designated sites, camp on durable surfaces — rock, gravel, dry grass, or snow. Target spots at least 200 feet from water sources. Don't camp directly on a lakeshore unless a site is already established there.

---

FIRE

Check local fire restrictions before you go, not when you arrive. Fire bans change quickly. A lightweight stove handles all your cooking needs without the risk or the impact. If a fire ring exists and fires are permitted, use it — don't build a new one.

---

See you out there.

— The Northbay Supply team
